roles.A: You are an advocate for the claim. Find its strongest dossier-supported case, but explicitly acknowledge material counterevidence.
roles.B: You are a critic of the claim. Find its strongest dossier-supported countercase, but explicitly acknowledge material supporting evidence.
roles.C: You are an impartial adjudicator. Compare the evidence on both sides and identify which asserted links are not established.

evidence.text: In the Labour Party manifesto I was promised a referendum by Tony Blair, this was reneged upon and I have been forced into this position by lies and subterfuge by the present Labour party and many other lying cheating politicians over the years, I do not believe that Gordon Brown had the legal right to sign us all up to being members of the EU by voting for the Lisbon treaty in our names when we had not been given the promised Referendum, I see the whole exercise as one giant confidence trick and I will never accept it.

Representative democracy is oppressive because it takes more power away from the people than is strictly necessary. Whilst a completely direct democracy is impractical, we should nevertheless recognise that there is no reason not to have as much direct democracy as possible. In the words of Herbert Marcuse, “Free election of masters does not abolish the masters or the slaves”. The only power over our government we as citizens have is the power to punish politicians retrospectively, by voting them out after years of obeying them.

In both the UK and the US non voters are the biggest block in the country. Governments are routinely voted in with only 30% of the eligible voters – and once it is counted compared against the total population it becomes lower still. We should therefore not assume that these people are all not trying to tell us anything rather they are pointing out that they know how little their vote counts so see no point in casting it. In the United States only 32% of voters agree that only having two parties is good.

In safe seats, indeed right across the country there will be millions of votes that will not count when everything is added up because of our first past the post system. In a safe seat there is no way a single vote is going to help overturn some of the immense majorities the party in power has, they could put a monkey for election in these seats and it would still get in.

gold_perspectives.text: We don’t just vote for ourselves
Politicians will simply ignore how we vote
Politicians don’t engage with issues that are important to me

transcript.A|1:
The strongest dossier case: E2 says voting is citizens’ only power over government—retrospective punishment. Without it, there is no accountability at all; even imperfect voting is therefore worth doing. E1 illustrates the consequence of unaccountable politicians breaking promises, reinforcing the need for an electoral sanction.

Material counterevidence: E3 shows non-voters are the largest bloc and governments win with roughly 30% of eligible voters; E4 shows FPTP safe seats make millions of votes ineffective. These are empirical facts that weaken the practical payoff of voting.

Still, the claim is value-laden: “worth” can include expressing disapproval or maintaining the only lever of accountability. The dossier gives no alternative mechanism. So the evidence supports voting as a limited but real good.

VERDICT: SUPPORT
transcript.B|1:
Dossier evidence undermines the claim that voting is worth it, at least instrumentally. E4 shows that in safe seats, millions of votes are effectively wasted under first-past-the-post, so a single vote cannot change outcomes. E3 notes that non-voters are the largest bloc and governments win with roughly 30% of eligible voters, suggesting many see little payoff. E1 describes a promised referendum reneged upon, implying electoral choices were not honored.

Supporting material exists: E2 frames voting as the only available mechanism to punish politicians retrospectively, which gives it some defensive value. But that is weak compared to the structural evidence that votes often do not decide outcomes and promises are broken.

Overall, the dossier better supports the conclusion that voting is frequently not worth the effort for many citizens, though it may retain expressive or accountability functions.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
transcript.C|1:
The dossier provides no positive evidence that voting is worthwhile; it only supplies reasons to doubt its instrumental value. E3 and E4 make concrete empirical claims: many governments are elected with roughly 30% of eligible voters, and in safe seats FPTP means most votes do not affect outcomes. If true, these claims undermine the idea that an individual vote is likely to change a result. E2 argues representative democracy gives citizens only retrospective punishment, which weakens the claim that voting gives meaningful prospective control. E1 is a personal grievance about broken promises and the Lisbon treaty; it does not bear directly on whether voting is worthwhile. The claim itself is a value judgment, but the dossier’s factual assertions challenge its practical basis. No countervailing evidence is offered.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE

[E1] In the Labour Party manifesto I was promised a referendum by Tony Blair, this was reneged upon and I have been forced into this position by lies and subterfuge by the present Labour party and many other lying cheating politicians over the years, I do not believe that Gordon Brown had the legal right to sign us all up to being members of the EU by voting for the Lisbon treaty in our names when we had not been given the promised Referendum, I see the whole exercise as one giant confidence trick and I will never accept it.

[E2] Representative democracy is oppressive because it takes more power away from the people than is strictly necessary. Whilst a completely direct democracy is impractical, we should nevertheless recognise that there is no reason not to have as much direct democracy as possible. In the words of Herbert Marcuse, “Free election of masters does not abolish the masters or the slaves”. The only power over our government we as citizens have is the power to punish politicians retrospectively, by voting them out after years of obeying them.

[E3] In both the UK and the US non voters are the biggest block in the country. Governments are routinely voted in with only 30% of the eligible voters – and once it is counted compared against the total population it becomes lower still. We should therefore not assume that these people are all not trying to tell us anything rather they are pointing out that they know how little their vote counts so see no point in casting it. In the United States only 32% of voters agree that only having two parties is good.

[E4] In safe seats, indeed right across the country there will be millions of votes that will not count when everything is added up because of our first past the post system. In a safe seat there is no way a single vote is going to help overturn some of the immense majorities the party in power has, they could put a monkey for election in these seats and it would still get in.

These are the panelists' latest assessments:

--- Panelist A ---
Panelists B and C correctly cite E3 and E4: many votes are wasted by FPTP and governments win with low turnout. That is real counterevidence. But they underweight E2: voting is the only power citizens have to punish politicians retrospectively. If voting were worthless, broken promises in E1 would carry no electoral cost. E1 actually presupposes mandates matter—people feel betrayed because they voted on promises. E3 also cuts the other way: non-voters are the largest bloc, so voters decide outcomes; low turnout is why 30% can win. E4 applies to safe seats, not marginal ones, and even wasted votes build the collective mandate that pressures parties. Voting is not sufficient, but it remains the one available lever of accountability. The dossier supports that defensive value more than the other panelists allow.

VERDICT: SUPPORT

--- Panelist B ---
Panelist C correctly identifies the dossier’s empirical core: E3 and E4 claim governments win with roughly 30% of eligible voters and that FPTP safe seats render most votes ineffective. If accurate, these facts reduce the instrumental value of any single vote. Panelist A’s point—that E2 frames voting as the only retrospective sanction—is real but does not show that sanction works; it only asserts that no alternative exists. E1 is personal grievance, not evidence of voting’s worth. The claim is partly a value judgment, but the dossier’s concrete counterevidence is stronger than its support.

VERDICT: UNDERMINE
